A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Moto research and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v2 includes supplementary Sections 7–10; much of this material matches implementation details and analyses previously presented in v1's main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion-token classification and prediction results, SIMPLER and CALVIN policy evaluations, and fine-tuning ablations in Tables 5–8 and Figures 10–12.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds physical-robot evaluations and human-video pretraining and transfer experiments in Figures 8–10.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the same tokenizer, autoregressive model, action-query mechanism, 50% attention masking, inference procedure, and joint losses. The new datasets and robot experiments use these existing components with experiment-specific training schedules.

E1.justification: v2 adds 105k SSV2 human videos to the robot-video pretraining coverage. It also adds physical FANUC robot evaluation on banana placement, laptop closing, and disassembly, including novel-object and visual-distractor scenarios. v1's policy evaluations cover SIMPLER and CALVIN only.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds OpenVLA fine-tuned on RT-1 Robot Action to the SIMPLER comparison in v1 Table 7. The original SIMPLER comparators, CALVIN comparator set, and Moto ablation variants remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces physical evaluation using 30 demonstrations per task and randomized test positions, together with mixed OXE/SSV2 pretraining and new adaptation budgets. It also revises the stated OXE sampling protocol: v1 Section 4.3 gives a uniform three-frame interval, whereas v2 Section 8.1 adjusts non-RT-1 subsets by frame rate. This reported revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds physical robustness tests with distractors and novel objects, a comparison isolating additional human-video pretraining, and human-to-robot motion-transfer visualizations in Figures 8–10. Supplementary Figure 16 adds rotation and stacking generation examples. The earlier data-efficiency and fine-tuning ablations remain.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies ten test repetitions per physical-robot task with randomized object positions in Sections 4 and 7.1. This adds repetition information for new experiments, without establishing increased repetitions of existing benchmarks. The existing likelihood bands remain, and no seeds, defined confidence intervals, or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: The matched SIMPLER and CALVIN scores remain unchanged. New results include fine-tuned OpenVLA's 0.349 overall SIMPLER score, physical-task averages of 60% for Moto versus 23.33% without motion tokens, and 78.3% Move Near success with OXE+SSV2 versus 60.4% with OXE alone. The latter is a new pretraining-condition comparison, not a same-setting improvement between versions.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 retain the same autoregressive objective, action-loss decomposition, and combined fine-tuning loss. No new formal definitions, assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations appear in the supplementary material.

C1.justification: Although the abstract and three methodological contributions remain, v2's introduction and conclusion explicitly claim demonstrated human-to-robot motion transfer and benefits from human-video pretraining. v1 presents human-motion learning as future work. This substantially extends the claimed scope beyond robot-video pretraining.

C2.justification: v2 softens the SIMPLER interpretation from surpassing larger models to comparable performance. It adds interpretations concerning physical robustness and human-motion transfer, including extrapolation to online human-demonstration learning. Supplementary Section 10 describes the SSV2 study as preliminary; most remaining future-work discussion is retained from v1 Section 6.

D1.justification: The core implementation and hyperparameter tables are retained in the supplement. v2 adds named OXE constituent datasets, human-video sampling details, and physical-robot adaptation schedules: 500 tokenizer steps, five additional pretraining epochs, and 20 fine-tuning epochs. It newly states that code is open source, while GPU descriptions lose the earlier A100 model designation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to pi0, CogACT, LAPO, DynaMo, and the Something-Something dataset, including explicit distinctions from LAPO's gaming focus and DynaMo's representation learning. Five background references are removed, including Flamingo and Prismatic VLMs. The central positioning around autoregressive motion tokens remains.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses the related-work and experimental narrative. Detailed setup, baseline descriptions, training information, and much of the old conclusion are reorganized into supplementary Sections 7–10, accompanied by shorter main-text Sections 4 and 6. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v2 merges the earlier overview and tokenizer diagrams into Figure 2, updates Figure 1 with human-video imagery, and adds physical-robot, human-transfer, and rotation/stacking displays. Existing benchmark illustrations, reconstruction examples, and technical tables move to the supplement. The SIMPLER table gains a comparator row, while retained plots are resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluates robot policies only in simulation and leaves human-video transfer as future work. v2 supplies physical deployment and robustness tests plus a direct human-video pretraining comparison, substantially strengthening evidence for the central video-to-control premise. The physical study remains small, quantitative human-video evaluation covers only Move Near, and uncertainty is not quantified; these constrain broad generalization claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation gained.
